opus-5.5.text:
For me, vision has never been just one subfield of AI. It's a way of asking what intelligence actually is.

There's a common view now, especially after large language models took off, that language is the core of intelligence. If you can model text well enough, you get reasoning, knowledge, maybe even something like understanding. I think that's partly true, but incomplete. Language is a very compressed, very human-made representation of the world. It's what we write down *after* we've already understood something. Vision is much closer to the raw signal. It's how animals, and babies before they can talk, build a model of the world in the first place.

So when I think about computer vision, I don't think of it as "recognize this cat" or "segment this car." Those were useful benchmarks for a while, but the deeper question is this: can a system, from high-dimensional, messy, continuous sensory input, figure out the structure of the world? Objects, space, physics, cause and effect, what persists over time. That's what perception really is. It isn't labeling. It's building an internal world model.

And that's hard in a way language isn't. With text, the tokens are already meaningful units that humans defined. With pixels, nothing is given to you. You have to discover what the units even are. In a sense, vision forces you to confront the grounding problem directly, and I think that's why it matters for intelligence.

There's also an evolutionary argument I find compelling. Vision appeared hundreds of millions of years ago, and some people link the Cambrian explosion to the emergence of eyes. Once organisms could see, they had to predict, plan, and act in a much richer environment. Language came very, very late. So if we take nature as a hint, perception and acting in the physical world is the foundation, and language sits on top of it.

That's why I sometimes say I'm a little contrarian right now. I don't think we'll reach truly general intelligence by scaling text alone. At some point the models have to see, and not just as a plug-in where you bolt an image encoder onto an LLM. Visual understanding has to be first-class, so the system learns about space, about the 3D world, about how things move and interact. Language can be an interface, a very powerful one, but the world model underneath has to be grounded in something like vision.

So in short, computer vision to me is the study of how intelligence comes from the world itself rather than from our descriptions of it. And I think we're still pretty early on that path.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That question is actually close to my heart, because I think people often misunderstand what computer vision is about. It's not really about building a system that can label a cat in a photo. It's about understanding how an intelligent agent perceives and makes sense of the physical world.

If you look at biological evolution, the eye came first, and then the brain grew around it. Language is a very recent invention. So when I think about intelligence, I don't think it starts from words. It starts from an agent that has to see, move, predict what happens next, and survive. Vision in that sense is not a modality you bolt onto a language model. It's the foundation of grounding.

That's why I always say that "visual intelligence" is a better framing than "computer vision." A camera gives you pixels, but pixels are not understanding. Understanding means building an internal model of space, of objects, of physics, of how things change over time. A child can do this long before they can speak. They know that if you push a cup off the table it falls, and they're surprised if it doesn't.

For me the interesting research question is: what does a model learn when it learns from visual data at scale, without language telling it what to see? When we worked on self-supervised learning, on things like DINO or MAE, the goal was exactly that. Can a system discover structure in the world purely by observing it? And it turns out it can learn a lot. But there's still a gap between recognizing things and really reasoning about the world, and closing that gap is what I spend most of my time on now.

So the short answer is, I see vision not as one application of AI but as a window into what intelligence fundamentally is. Language gives us a compressed description of the world written by humans. Vision gives us the world itself. If we want AI that can actually act in that world, we can't skip that part.

astra-6.text:
I think computer vision gives us a very concrete way to study intelligence. You can ask: how does a system take the light arriving at a camera and turn it into an understanding of the world? That sounds like a perception problem, but it quickly becomes a problem about learning, reasoning, and prior knowledge.

For example, if you see a chair partially hidden behind a table, you don’t experience it as disconnected patches of color. You understand that there is a whole object there, that it occupies space, and that you could sit on it. There’s a lot packed into that seemingly effortless act of seeing.

So I see vision as a window into intelligence, rather than just a collection of tasks like image classification or object detection. Those tasks give us useful ways to measure progress, but the deeper question is how a system develops representations that let it understand and interact with its environment. Vision is particularly interesting because it connects abstract concepts to a physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computer vision gives us a very concrete way to study intelligence. You have a stream of pixels, but what you want to understand is the world behind those pixels: what objects are there, how they relate to each other, what is changing, and what might happen next. That gap between the input and the understanding is really interesting.

For me, vision is also a way to ask what it means to learn a useful representation. Recognizing an object is one test, but can the same representation help you understand a scene, follow motion, or guide an action? That pushes us beyond treating vision as a collection of separate recognition tasks.

I wouldn’t say vision alone is intelligence. But it is a rich place to investigate how intelligence connects to the physical world. You can build a system, give it visual experience, and ask very concrete questions about what it has actually learned and where its understanding breaks down.
